t: Ash.Type.Keyword casts client input as trusted stored data, bypassing the input validation of its field types
d: Improper Input Validation vulnerability in ash-project ash allows an attacker to bypass the input validation of the field types of a :keyword attribute or argument. Ash.Type.Keyword.cast_input/2 in lib/ash/type/keyword.ex converts a map input to a keyword list in try_map_to_keyword/2, which casts each declared field with Ash.Type.cast_stored/3. That function is meant for trusted values read back from the data layer, so client input skips the cast_input/2 of each field type. apply_constraints/2 casts the result again with cast_input/2, but most types accept a value of their own type unchanged. An embedded resource field is built without its create action, so its validations and changes do not run and its non-public attributes can be set. A :function field accepts a capture string such as &Mod.fun/1, and a :term field decodes Erlang external term format. This issue affects ash: from 3.24.0 before 3.38.1.

t: Unbounded Converter Memoisation in twig/markdown-extra Keyed on Template-Controlled Options
d: The html_to_markdown filter of twig/markdown-extra keeps an HtmlConverter for each distinct mapping of options it receives. They're kept in a static array, with no size limit and no eviction. The options are an argument of the filter. A template that passes options taken from the input, or a sandboxed template, can therefore make this cache grow without limit. The cache outlives the environment, so it fills the memory of long-running workers. The cache now keeps at most 100 converters, like the formatter caches of IntlExtension.

t: Sandbox Tag Allow-List Bypass via the Branch of a `guard` Tag That Isn't Selected
d: The guard tag compiles only one of its branches, depending on whether a callable exists. The other branch was still parsed, though. The extends, use, macro and block tags in it registered their effects on the template. The sandbox doesn't see these tags, since that branch isn't compiled. A sandboxed template allowed to use guard could therefore extend a template, import blocks and define macros, while the policy doesn't allow these tags: {% guard filter upper %}{% else %}{% extends "parent.html" %}{% endguard %} The templates reached this way come from the loader of the sandbox, and they are sandboxed too. What the branch that isn't selected registers on the parser is now discarded.

t: Missing autoescaping for a variable named like a macro import alias of another scope
d: The escaper considered x.attr, x['key'] and x.method() safe whenever {% import ... as x %} appeared anywhere in the template. Macro calls haven't needed this rule since Twig 3.0. It only matched ordinary variables that have the name of an alias imported in another block or macro, and printed them without escaping: {% block header %}{% import _self as item %}{{ item.hello() }}{% endblock %} {% block content %}{% for item in items %}{{ item.body }}{% endfor %}{% endblock %} Here, item.body is printed raw. This leads to XSS when the value comes from an attacker. The same happens with an import in a macro and an argument of the same name in another macro. It also happens with a template-level import placed after the block that uses the name. The rule is removed. Macro calls through an alias are still considered safe.

t: Sandboxed templates can rewrite application-owned `Markup` objects through their constructor
d: The sandbox allows every method of Twig\Markup objects, including their public constructor. A sandboxed template can therefore call __construct() on any Markup object that it reaches, and replace its content: {% do banner.__construct('<script>alert(1)</script>', 'UTF-8') %} A template gains nothing by rewriting its own output. The impact is on the Markup objects that come from the application and are also rendered elsewhere, like a global in a long-running worker. Their new content then ends up in trusted pages that aren't sandboxed. The sandbox no longer allows calling the constructor of Markup objects.

t: Sandbox property allow-list bypass via `html_cva()` variant values
d: Cva::apply() converted the values of variants, default variants and compound variants with (array). These values come from the arguments of html_cva(). A sandboxed template could therefore pass any object of its context, and print the private and protected properties of that object: {{ html_cva('base', {c: {p: user}}).apply({c: 'p'}) }} Variant maps that are ArrayAccess objects were also read with a key that the template chooses, without the property check of the sandbox. The template then printed the offsets that the object returned. Applications are affected when the sandbox allows the html_cva function and the apply method of Twig\Extra\Html\Cva. A value that isn't an array is now treated as a single item, so objects are dropped and never match a variant. Variant maps are also only used when they're arrays.

t: Sandbox property allow-list bypass via the `join` filter on non-iterable objects
d: The join filter converted a value that isn't iterable with (array) $value. For an object, that gives every property, including the private and protected ones. A sandboxed template allowed to use join could therefore print properties that the policy denies, and that templates can't read otherwise: {{ user|join(',') }} A value that isn't iterable is now joined as a single item. A Stringable object prints its checked string, and other objects throw, as with the first and last filters.

t: Sandbox allow-list and `__toString()` bypass via a dynamic `embed` parent expression
d: When the parent of an embed tag was an expression other than a string or a variable, the sandbox didn't see that expression. The functions, filters and tests of the expression weren't checked against the policy, and neither were its conversions to strings. A sandboxed template allowed to use embed could therefore call any function, filter or test, and any __toString() method: {% embed 'leak_' ~ app_secret() %}{% endembed %} Method calls and property reads were not affected, since they're checked at runtime. The sandbox now checks the parent expression of embed like any other expression of the template.

t: Sandbox `__toString()` policy bypass via spread arguments
d: Since Twig 3.28.0, the sandbox skips the toString() check of an argument whose PHP parameter can't hold a string, like an int. A spread argument was mapped to a single parameter, although it fills every parameter from its position on. A sandboxed template could therefore call a denied toString() method: {{ tag(...[1, obj]) }} Here, the first parameter of tag() is an int, and a later one accepts strings. Applications are affected when they allow such a function, filter or test in the sandbox. No built-in callable is affected. A spread argument is now checked unless every parameter that it can fill has a safe type.

t: Sandbox `__toString()` policy bypass via assignment and destructuring expressions
d: The sandbox checks that a template may call toString() on an object before converting it to a string. Since Twig 3.23.0, assignments like x = obj, and the destructuring forms [a] = list and {a} = obj, evaluate to the value that they assign. The sandbox didn't check that value, so a sandboxed template could call a denied toString() method: {{ (x = obj) }} {{ ({secret: s} = obj)|join }} No tag needs to be allowed. The sandbox now checks the result of assignments like the result of filters and functions. {% do x = obj %} and {% if (x = obj) %} still work, since they don't convert the value to a string.

t: Sandbox `__toString()` policy bypass via the input of custom tests
d: The sandbox checks that a template may call toString() on an object before converting it to a string. It didn't check the input of tests. The PHP callable of a test may convert this input to a string, for example when its parameter is typed as string. PHP then calls toString() on an object without the sandbox checking it first: {{ obj is upperish }} Applications are affected when they register such a test and allow it in the sandbox. No built-in test is affected. The sandbox now checks the input of tests like the input of filters. The built-in tests that never convert their input to a string still skip the check.

t: Sandbox `__toString()` policy bypass via the `is true` test
d: The sandbox checks that a template may call toString() on an object before converting it to a string. For an object, the is true test evaluates to the object itself, and that result wasn't checked. A sandboxed template could therefore print an object through a denied toString() method: {{ obj is true }} The same applies when the result is concatenated or passed to a filter. No tag needs to be allowed. A test in a boolean context, like {% if obj is true %}, isn't affected, since it doesn't convert the object to a string. The sandbox now checks the result of tests like the result of filters and functions.

t: Type confusion via structural idempotency guard in ExAws.Dynamo.Encoder.encode/2
d: Improper Validation of Specified Type of Input in ExAws.Dynamo.Encoder.encode/2 in ex_aws_dynamo allows an attacker who controls map data passed into a DynamoDB call to choose the raw stored DynamoDB AttributeValue. The encode/2 function in lib/ex_aws/dynamo/encoder.ex has one clause per DynamoDB type descriptor ("S", "N", "B", "BOOL", "M", "L", "NS", "SS", "BS", "NULL") that treats any map merely containing such a key as already encoded and returns it verbatim, bypassing the ExAws.Dynamo.Encodable protocol. The match is on the presence of the key alone, so no check is made that the value is well formed for the claimed type, and extra keys and arbitrary nested content survive untouched. An application that threads user-influenced map data (a decoded JSON body, a nested attribute, or an expression_attribute_values entry) into a Dynamo write or query therefore lets the user, rather than the application, decide the stored attribute's declared type, its bytes, and its structure. This type confusion breaks round-trip integrity and enables silent persistent data corruption, injection of attributes and raw binaries the schema never sanctioned, subversion of application authorization checks that trust the decoded type of a value, and a decoder crash on read-back that denies reads of the affected item to other users of the same table. This issue affects ex_aws_dynamo: from 2.0.0 before 4.3.0.

t: ex_aws_kms defaults RSA key-material wrapping to PKCS#1 v1.5 in get_parameters_for_import/3
d: Use of RSA Algorithm without OAEP vulnerability in ex-aws ex_aws_kms (ExAws.KMS module) causes callers who import external key material to wrap their secret KMS key material with the deprecated PKCS#1 v1.5 padding scheme by default. This vulnerability is associated with program file lib/ex_aws/kms.ex and program routine ExAws.KMS.get_parameters_for_import/3. ExAws.KMS.get_parameters_for_import/3 defaults its wrapping_algorithm argument to "RSAES_PKCS1_V1_5". AWS KMS returns this value as the WrappingAlgorithm for the import operation, and it dictates the RSA padding scheme the caller uses to wrap (RSA-encrypt) their secret key material before calling ImportKeyMaterial. AWS KMS also supports the stronger RSAES_OAEP_SHA_1 and RSAES_OAEP_SHA_256 schemes. By defaulting to RSAES_PKCS1_V1_5, the library steers callers who do not explicitly override the argument toward the weakest of the three. PKCS#1 v1.5 encryption padding is susceptible to Bleichenbacher adaptive chosen-ciphertext (padding oracle) attacks, which can recover the wrapped plaintext without the private key given an oracle that reveals whether a decrypted value was validly padded. Because the unwrap happens inside AWS KMS, which does not expose a padding oracle, the practical exploitability is low and this is a defense-in-depth weakness. Callers can avoid the weak default by explicitly passing "RSAES_OAEP_SHA_256" (or "RSAES_OAEP_SHA_1") as the wrapping algorithm. This issue affects ex_aws_kms: from 2.1.0 before 2.7.0.

t: ex_aws normalizes .. in S3 object keys client-side, allowing bucket or key-prefix escape
d: Relative path traversal in ex_aws allows an attacker who controls an S3 object key to escape the intended bucket or key prefix. When ex_aws builds a path-style S3 request, ExAws.Operation.S3.add_bucket_to_path/2 in lib/ex_aws/operation/s3.ex joins the bucket name and the object key into a single path string and then normalizes it, collapsing . and .. segments the way a filesystem path would. Because the bucket is the first segment of the combined string, a leading ../ in the object key pops the bucket off the path. With bucket mybucket and a key of ../victim/secret.txt, the combined /mybucket/../victim/secret.txt normalizes to /victim/secret.txt, so the request (signed with the application's own credentials) is sent to bucket victim. The same mechanism collapses ../ within a key, defeating any isolation an application enforces by prepending a trusted prefix. Only the default path-style configuration is affected; requests built with virtual_host: true do not run this normalization. Because S3 treats object keys as opaque and does not resolve .. itself, the client-side normalization introduces a traversal that would not otherwise exist. Any application that derives an S3 object key from untrusted input and relies on the bucket, or a key prefix, as a tenant or trust boundary is exposed to cross-bucket or cross-prefix read and write, depending on the operation and the credentials' permissions. This issue affects ex_aws: from 2.1.7 before 2.8.0.

t: IMDSv2 metadata token request follows HTTP redirects in ex_aws
d: Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) vulnerability in ex_aws (instance metadata token provider). This vulnerability is associated with program files lib/ex_aws/instance_meta_token_provider.ex and program routines ExAws.InstanceMetaTokenProvider.request_token/1 and ExAws.InstanceMetaTokenProvider.get/1. ex_aws requests its IMDSv2 session token from the link-local metadata endpoint (http://169.254.169.254/latest/api/token) with HTTP redirect following enabled. Because the token request follows 3xx redirects and does not restrict the redirect target to the link-local range, an attacker who can influence the response to the metadata request (for example an on-segment neighbor spoofing the link-local address) can answer with a redirect to an arbitrary host. The library follows the redirect and accepts the arbitrary host's response body as the IMDSv2 session token, caching it and sending it as the x-aws-ec2-metadata-token header on every subsequent metadata and credential request. This issue affects ex_aws: from 2.3.0 before 2.8.0.

t: Apache BuildStream: symlink following via plugin API
d: UNIX symbolic link (symlink) following vulnerability in Apache BuildStream allows source plugins to inadvertently read or write files on the host, with the privileges of the user running BuildStream, via symlinks from malicious or compromised source archives or respositories, as part of source fetching. The impact of this issue is mitigated by: * BuildStream projects should only use trusted sources in their elements as otherwise the build output can also not be trusted * None of the source plugins in the buildstream, buildstream-plugins or buildstream-plugins-community repositories use the vulnerable `open_file` method This issue affects Apache BuildStream: through 2.8.1. Users are recommended to upgrade to version 2.8.2, which fixes the issue.

t: Apache BuildStream: path traversal via unvalidated CAS Directory
d: Improper limitation of a pathname to a restricted directory ('path traversal') vulnerability in Apache BuildStream allows malicious or compromised artifact or execution servers to write files on the host, with the privileges of the user running BuildStream, as part of `bst artifact checkout`. The impact of this issue is mitigated by: * BuildStream projects should only use trusted servers for remote cache and remote execution as otherwise the build output can also not be trusted This issue affects Apache BuildStream: through 2.8.1. Users are recommended to upgrade to version 2.8.2, which fixes the issue.

t: S3 object key query-string injection and truncation via unencoded reserved characters in ex_aws
d: Improper Encoding or Escaping of Output vulnerability in ex_aws (S3 request URL construction). This vulnerability is associated with program files lib/ex_aws/request/url.ex and program routines ExAws.Request.Url.build/2, ExAws.Request.Url.sanitize/2 and ExAws.Request.Url.get_path/2. ex_aws does not percent-encode reserved characters in S3 object keys when it assembles the request URL. A literal ? in an object key survives unencoded: build/2 inserts the operation path verbatim and URI.to_string/1 emits it without encoding, and sanitize/2 then splits the flattened URL on the first ?, treating everything after it as the query string. Because the split runs before uri_encode is applied to the path, the ? is never neutralized, and the recovered query is re-inserted without any encoding. An attacker who controls part of an object key (for example a download or upload keyed by a user-supplied filename) can therefore truncate the key past application-appended suffixes, causing the request to address a different object than the application intended, and can inject live S3 sub-resource operations (such as ?acl, ?tagging or ?versions) into the request. The manipulated URL is signed and transmitted normally, so the tampering is authorized like any legitimate request. This issue affects ex_aws: from 2.1.2 before 2.8.0.

If the file can be ingested using the destination table’s schema and input format, users with query access to that table can read its contents. Upgrade to Apache Pinot 1.6.0 and keep controller.ingestFromURI.allowLocalFileSystem at its default value of false on every controller. Until you can upgrade, block the URI ingestion endpoint if it is unused or restrict it to trusted operators.

t: Unbounded Out-of-Order Fragment Reassembly in QUIC Streams
d: Issue summary: A QUIC peer that sends many small out-of-order STREAM fragments while withholding the first byte of the stream may cause OpenSSL to buffer a large number of reassembly nodes occupying much larger memory than the actual data sent. Impact summary: A remote peer can pin large amounts of memory on a server that accepts incoming QUIC streams, potentially exhausting memory and causing Denial of Service. CWE: CWE-770: Allocation of Resources Without Limits or Throttling Description: QUIC receive flow control limits the highest byte offset a peer may reach on a stream. It does not limit how many out-of-order fragments the receiver buffers. OpenSSL allocates a reassembly node for each non-adjacent STREAM fragment and never caps the count. A peer that opens a stream and sends many one-byte fragments at increasing offsets, while withholding the first byte, makes the receiver retain one node per fragment without delivering any data. Only applications that accept incoming streams are exposed. With the default policy, which rejects peer-initiated streams, the stream is torn down before state accumulates. Because the read side never advances past the missing prefix, the flow control window never slides and the nodes stay pinned for the life of the connection. The per-stream window bounds the highest offset, so the memory one stream can pin is finite, but it can reach tens of megabytes and, across many streams and connections, drive memory pressure and Denial of Service. The severity is limited because the exhaustion is bounded by flow control and requires a non-default configuration. FIPS impact: no The affected code is outside the FIPS module boundary.

t: Apache Texera: Missing authorization when adding public projects
d: Missing Authorization vulnerability in the public project REST API of Apache Texera (incubating). The public project API did not check that a project had been made public before granting the caller read access to it. Any authenticated user with an approved account (the REGULAR or ADMIN role; new accounts need administrator approval by default) could give themselves lasting read access to other users' private projects and to the private workflows in them, including their version and execution history. Only deployments in which users have created projects are affected; the project feature is hidden in the web UI by default. This issue affects Apache Texera: from 1.1.0-incubating before 1.3.0-incubating. Users are recommended to upgrade to version 1.3.0-incubating, which fixes the issue by removing the deprecated project feature and its data. If you cannot upgrade immediately, configure the reverse proxy in front of Texera to reject every request whose path starts with /api/project, /api/public/project or /api/access/project, and every request whose path contains ';', which the Texera server ignores when routing. Respond with 403 or 404, not 401: from 1.2.0-incubating the web UI treats a 401 as an expired session, and the workflow pages request the project list when they load. Unless an administrator has enabled the project feature, this does not affect other functionality; those project-list requests are simply rejected. Make sure the Texera server is reachable only through that proxy. Blocking and upgrading do not undo access obtained earlier. Before upgrading, review the project_user_access table, which remains empty unless someone has used the feature: treat any READ grant on a project that is not listed in public_project, and that the project's owner did not give, as suspect. The upgrade deletes this table. Removing a grant does not remove copies the user may already have made of the workflows.

The project feature is hidden in the web UI by default, but the API was reachable regardless of that setting. This issue affects Apache Texera: from 1.1.0-incubating before 1.3.0-incubating. Users are recommended to upgrade to version 1.3.0-incubating, which fixes the issue by removing the deprecated project feature and its data. If you cannot upgrade immediately, configure the reverse proxy in front of Texera to reject every request whose path starts with /api/project, /api/public/project or /api/access/project, and every request whose path contains ';', which the Texera server ignores when routing. Unless an administrator has enabled the project feature, this does not affect other functionality; those project-list requests are simply rejected. Make sure the Texera server is reachable only through that proxy. Blocking and upgrading do not undo access obtained earlier. Before upgrading, review the project, project_user_access and workflow_of_project tables, which remain empty unless someone has used the feature, and remove rows you do not expect; the upgrade deletes these tables. Do not copy project grants into workflow_user_access without checking each one.

t: Apache Texera: Missing authorization on the computing unit workflow websocket

In local JVM and single-node Docker Compose deployments this is possible directly; in Kubernetes deployments it is possible from code running inside another computing unit in the cluster. This issue affects Apache Texera : from 1.1.0 through 1.2.0. Users are recommended to upgrade to version 1.3.0, which fixes the issue. Local JVM and Docker Compose deployments do not provide the full security model and should only be used by trusted users.

t: Apache Texera: The DELETE /api/quota/deleteCollection/{eid} endpoint does not require authentication, allowing an unauthenticated user to delete workflow execut

t: Apache Texera: Missing authentication on the Python virtual environment endpoints in non-Kubernetes deployments
d: Missing Authentication for Critical Function in Apache Texera (incubating). The Python virtual environment (PVE) management endpoints of a computing unit are not authenticated by the application itself. In the local JVM and single-node Docker Compose deployments, which place no authenticating gateway in front of the services, these endpoints are reachable without credentials. The Kubernetes deployment gates them at the gateway, so only the Kubernetes deployment provides the full security model described in SECURITY.md. This issue affects Apache Texera (incubating): from 1.1.0 through 1.2.0. Users are recommended to use the Kubernetes deployment, which enforces the full security model, and to upgrade to 1.3.0-incubating, which documents that the local JVM and single-node Docker Compose deployments do not provide the full security model and should only be used by trusted users.

t: Apache StormCrawler: Server-Side Request Forgery and Cross-Origin Credential Disclosure via robots.txt Redirect Handling
d: Description When StormCrawler fetches a host's `/robots.txt` and receives a redirect, `HttpRobotRulesParser` resolves the `Location` header and re-fetches the target for up to five hops. The loop checks neither the scheme, the host nor the port of the resolved target, and it is not governed by `http.allow.redirects`, which only affects the page fetch. A crawled site can therefore point the robots.txt fetch at any address reachable from the fetcher worker, including loopback interfaces, private ranges and cloud metadata endpoints. Every crawled URL triggers a robots.txt fetch on a cache miss, so no unusual configuration is required to reach the loop. The fetched body is only parsed as robots rules and is not returned to the caller, so the read itself is blind. The more direct impact is on credentials: the okhttp protocol applies its configured request headers, including the `Authorization` header built from `http.basicauth.user` and `http.basicauth.password` and anything in `http.custom.headers`, to every request it makes. Because StormCrawler follows the redirect itself and issues a new request, okhttp's own removal of the `Authorization` header across a host change does not apply, and the operator's crawl credentials are delivered to the host the redirect names. The connection-time IP filter, `http.filter.ipaddress.include` and `http.filter.ipaddress.exclude`, is installed as an okhttp network interceptor on the same client and does apply to these hops when it is configured. It ships with no rules, which is why the path is reachable in a default configuration. URL filtering never applies, because the robots.txt fetch does not pass through the outlink filter chain. Mitigation Upgrade to 4.0.0, where a robots.txt redirect is followed only when the target uses http or https and shares scheme, host and port with the URL it was reached from. Deployments that legitimately serve robots.txt through a cross-host redirect can restore the previous behaviour with `http.robots.redirect.crosshost.allow`. Users who cannot upgrade immediately should set `http.filter.ipaddress.exclude` to cover loopback, private, link-local and CGNAT ranges, which is enforced after DNS resolution and therefore also on redirect hops. Operators who configure `http.basicauth.*` or `http.custom.headers` for a crawl should assume those credentials may have been sent to third-party hosts and rotate them, and should scope credentials by running a separate topology per origin. Credit Independently reported to the Apache StormCrawler PMC by n0mi1k, with a proof of concept. Also found by the ASF -- using Claude agents to study the security of open-source projects, validated and reported by Apache StormCrawler.

t: Apache StormCrawler: Crawled Content Injects Crawler Control Metadata via the SQL Status Store
d: Description The SQL status backend serialises per-URL metadata into a single column by concatenating a tabulation, the key, an equals sign and the value, with no escaping. On read-back the string is split on the same two characters, so the round trip is not injective: a value that contains a tabulation returns as one or more additional keys that were never written. Values on that path are supplied by crawled servers. `FetcherBolt` records the raw `Location` header of a redirect as `_redirTo`, and `_redirTo` is part of the default `metadata.persist` set, so a redirect whose `Location` contains a tabulation followed by `key=value` pairs introduces those keys into the crawler's own control metadata on the next scheduling cycle. Several control keys are read without a prefix, so the injected keys are live: `http.proxy.host`, `http.proxy.port`, `http.proxy.user` and `http.proxy.pass` among them, as well as scheduling and request-shaping keys such as `depth`, `max.depth`, `crawl.delay`, `http.content.limit` and `isSitemap`. Where a proxy manager is configured, the consequence is not limited to corrupted scheduling data. `SingleProxyManager.getProxy(Metadata)` consults the per-URL metadata first and returns what it finds, so an injected proxy host and port take precedence over the operator's configured proxy and subsequent fetches, together with any configured `Authorization` header, are routed through a host the crawled content chose. A related defect in `AbstractStatusUpdaterBolt` compounds this: an injected `status.store.as.is.with.nextfetchdate` that is not a valid instant escapes the enclosing try/catch and stops the bolt, and because the stored row is replayed the failure repeats. Deployments using the OpenSearch or Solr status backends are unaffected, because those serialise metadata structurally. Mitigation Upgrade to 4.0.0, where the metadata column is written in an escaped form behind a format marker, rows written by earlier versions are still decoded unchanged, and the stored next-fetch-date is parsed defensively. The fix does not repair rows written before the upgrade. Operators using the SQL status backend should inspect the metadata column of an existing status table for tabulation characters and remove the affected rows, and should assume any proxy credentials configured for the crawl may have been exercised through an attacker-chosen proxy and rotate them. Users who cannot upgrade immediately can remove `_redirTo` from `metadata.persist` to close the demonstrated path, though other crawled values reaching persisted metadata remain. Credit Independently reported to the Apache StormCrawler PMC by n0mi1k, with a proof of concept. Also found by the ASF -- using Claude agents to study the security of open-source projects, validated and reported by Apache StormCrawler.

t: Apache StormCrawler: Host-Only Cookies Sent to Any Host
d: Description `CookieConverter.getCookies` decides which stored cookies to attach to an outbound request. The applicability check is nested inside a test for the presence of a `Domain` attribute, so a cookie without one, which is the ordinary form of a session cookie, skips scoping entirely and is returned for whatever target URL was passed. RFC 6265 requires the opposite: a cookie with no `Domain` attribute is host-only and belongs to the host that set it. Two further defects sit in the same method. The domain comparison has no notion of a registrable domain, so a `Domain` value of `com` matches every host under it, and the comparison returns true when it throws, so a failure to evaluate the check admits the cookie. Neither the converter nor `MetadataTransfer`, which carries the stored cookie to outlinks, ever considers the host that issued it. Cookie handling is opt-in: it requires `http.use.cookies` to be set to true, which is not the default, and the cookie key to be listed in `metadata.transfer`. The documented recipe does not work as written, because the `metadata.transfer` example in the internals documentation names `set-cookie` while the key present in metadata is `protocol.set-cookie` and the transfer matches key names exactly. Deployments affected are therefore those where an operator determined the correct key, enabled cookie handling and crawls an authenticated site whose pages link or redirect to other hosts. In that case the session cookie of the authenticated origin is sent to those hosts. Mitigation Upgrade to 4.0.0, where a cookie without a `Domain` attribute is sent only to the host that set it, a single-label domain is rejected and the domain check fails closed. Because the protocol does not yet record the host that issued a cookie, cookies without a `Domain` attribute are not sent at all until that host is recorded; operators relying on cookie transfer will notice this. The documentation error is corrected in the same release. Users who cannot upgrade immediately should confine an authenticated crawl to a topology whose URL filters keep it on the origin that issued the credentials, and should not rely on cookie scoping as a boundary. Rotating session credentials used for such crawls is advisable. Credit Independently reported to the Apache StormCrawler PMC by n0mi1k, with a proof of concept. Also found by the ASF -- using Claude agents to study the security of open-source projects, validated and reported by Apache StormCrawler.

t: Apache StormCrawler: HostURLFilter Domain Scoping Silently Disabled by a Wrong Variable Check
d: Description `HostURLFilter.configure` reads the `ignoreOutsideDomain` parameter but tests the node belonging to `ignoreOutsideHost` when deciding whether the domain mode was configured. A filter configuration that names only `ignoreOutsideDomain`, which the class documentation presents as an independent mode, is therefore discarded: the flag is forced to false, `filter` short-circuits on its guard and every URL is returned unchanged. The filter enforces nothing while appearing to be configured, and the failure is silent. The mirror-image configuration, naming only `ignoreOutsideHost`, fails with a `NullPointerException` while the topology is starting. The effect is the loss of a scope control the operator configured, so a crawled page's outlinks are followed to hosts the operator intended to exclude. Impact beyond crawl scope depends on what the crawler then fetches and is not claimed here. Projects generated from the StormCrawler Maven archetypes are not affected, because all three shipped filter configurations set both parameters. Mitigation Upgrade to 4.0.0, where each parameter is tested independently. Operators whose configuration sets only `ignoreOutsideDomain` will find the crawl restricted to the source domain, as configured, which may reduce the number of outlinks accepted. Users who cannot upgrade immediately should set both `ignoreOutsideHost` and `ignoreOutsideDomain` explicitly in the `HostURLFilter` configuration, which produces the intended behaviour on affected versions. Credit Independently reported to the Apache StormCrawler PMC by n0mi1k, with a proof of concept. Also found by the ASF -- using Claude agents to study the security of open-source projects, validated and reported by Apache StormCrawler.

t: Multiple Vulnerabilities in GlobalEduca's Job Portal

The portal serves the file via a GET request to ‘/attachments/{attachment_id}’ with the ‘Content-Disposition: inline’ header, so it can be opened in the browser’s PDF viewer during review. t: SUSE NeuVector DLP/WAF rule inside every documented validation limit overflows a 2048-byte stack buffer in the enforcer dataplane

t: TypesenseVectorStore doDelete filter injection via document ID allows unintended document deletion
d: TypesenseVectorStore is vulnerable to a document ID injection in its delete operation that can cause unintended documents to be deleted. TypesenseVectorStore.doDelete(List<String>) builds a Typesense filter_by expression by raw string concatenation of caller-supplied document IDs into the form id: [id1,id2,...] . The Typesense id field uses bare (unquoted) values in this list form with no escaping mechanism. An ID containing characters with syntactic meaning in the Typesense filter grammar — such as a comma ( , ), a closing bracket ( ] ), or operator tokens ( || , && ) — can break out of the list literal and alter the structure of the filter expression. An attacker who controls a document ID passed to the delete operation can use this to delete documents other than the intended ones (comma injection), or to construct a filter that matches every document in the collection (operator breakout), resulting in unintended bulk deletion. Applications that pass externally supplied or user-controlled document IDs to VectorStore.delete(List<String>) backed by TypesenseVectorStore are affected.

t: An SQL injection vulnerability was found in the ADM Defender of ADM
d: An SQL injection vulnerability exists in the firewall management component of ADM Defender due to insufficient validation and improper handling of input data in SQLite queries. This vulnerability may allow an attacker with access to the affected functionality to manipulate database queries, potentially resulting in unauthorized access to or modification of firewall-related data. Affected products and versions include: from ADM 4.1.0 through ADM 4.3.3.RY62 as well as from ADM 5.0.0 through ADM 5.1.4.RM62.

t: An improper authorization vulnerability was found in the Wallpaper Component of ADM
d: An improper authorization vulnerability exists in the wallpaper component of ADM. An authenticated, low-privileged user can bypass shared-folder access controls by specifying an image path within a restricted share. The CGI processes the request with root privileges without enforcing the source share's access permissions, allowing the attacker to copy and retrieve images they are not authorized to access, resulting in unauthorized information disclosure. Affected products and versions include: from ADM 4.1.0 through ADM 4.3.3.RY62 as well as from ADM 5.0.0 through ADM 5.1.4.RM62.
